title: Jogen Chowdhury Turned Memory Dream And Everyday Life Into Art
excerpt: An Ina Puri extract in Hindustan Times returns to the painter's own credo — his memories, dreams and immediate environment as his subjects — as India mourns the artist, who died in Kolkata at 87.
body:
• Jogen Chowdhury, who died in Kolkata on Sunday, October 25 at 87, built his art from his own life: "My memories, my dreams, my thoughts, my environment — they could all become subjects of my works."
  • Ina Puri's writing on Chowdhury, excerpted by Hindustan Times, reads his distorted figures as a deliberate way to show the complexity inside a person and in relationships.
  • Born in Faridpur in 1939 and displaced to a Kolkata refugee colony in 1948, he studied in Paris, kept the art collection at Rashtrapati Bhavan, taught at Santiniketan and sat in the Rajya Sabha.
  • His cross-hatched line, developed at art college and carried into the Reminiscences of a Dream series, made everyday objects — a bed, pots, spoons, textiles — into art.

Jogen Chowdhury explained his method in one sentence, and it is the sentence an Ina Puri extract published by Hindustan Times puts at the centre of his work: "My memories, my dreams, my thoughts, my environment — they could all become subjects of my works." The line, quoted in Sotheby's essay on the artist from his book Enigmatic Visions, was written after his return from Paris, when he decided his art could be built neither by copying Western art nor by falling back on ancient Indian heritage alone. His own characteristics would define it.

The extract has been widely read this week because Chowdhury died on Sunday, October 25, at 87. Hindustan Times reported he had been treated for cancer, was hospitalised with a urinary tract infection, and was put on a ventilator on Saturday. He is survived by his wife, Shipra, and son, Soumya. Hospital sources told IANS he had cancer for the past 14 months and was undergoing chemotherapy before he fell ill on October 16.

A refugee childhood became the material

Chowdhury was born on February 16, 1939, in Daharpara village in Faridpur, in what is now Bangladesh. His mother made alpana, the traditional decorative floor painting, and he took his interest in drawing from her. In 1948, at nine years old, the family arrived in Calcutta from East Pakistan as refugees and settled in a refugee colony in south Calcutta. In The Punch Magazine, he said: "Since my childhood, I was a keen observer of people, their gestures and facial expressions. My relationship with people and my environment was deep and became part of my artworks."

He graduated from the Government College of Art and Craft, Calcutta, in 1960, taught at Howrah Zilla School on Rs 125 a month, and in 1965 went to Paris on a French government scholarship, winning the Prix de la Jeune Peinture in 1966.

The line, the distortion and the everyday

Chowdhury's signature is cross-hatching — dense, overlapping lines that build volume and shade. He developed the technique in the upper classes of art college and took it up seriously in 1968-69 with the Reminiscences of a Dream series in Madras, producing works such as Tiger in the Moonlit Night and Her Silver Throne. Sotheby's traces the darkness in those works to the refugee years: "We did not have electricity in our house and I had to read by the hurricane lantern. I had to fall back on black and white because we did not have enough light."

Puri's essay, quoted in The Punch Magazine from an exhibition catalogue, argues the distortion of his figures was a deliberate device to show "the complexity that exists within a man and in his relationship with the environment and the world." She returns often to his couples — faces that "reveal weariness as if the lovers of yesterday are long past their prime and their romance is now like a dried flower discovered between pages of a book of poems." For Chowdhury, everyday objects also had to be made artistic: "An object of use, like a bed, a light stand, pots, spoons, textiles, available in most households, may have artistic form, colour, line, etc and can give pleasure to the person who uses and looks at it."

The institution builder

He worked as a textile designer in Madras, was Keeper of Art at Rashtrapati Bhavan from 1972 to 1987, then taught at Kala Bhavan in Santiniketan, where he became principal. He sat in the Rajya Sabha for the Trinamool Congress from 2014 to 2020, and in 2019 opened Charubasona, his centre for arts in Kolkata, with the ground floor given to younger artists.

His student Ushmita Sahu, now director of Emami Art in Kolkata, told Hindustan Times: "As an artist, he showed us that a single line could hold the whole weight of a life, with its tenderness, irony and quiet unease." A Kiran Nadar Museum retrospective planned for February 2027 will now be a memorial too.

nri_angle: For the diaspora, Chowdhury's refugee-to-Kolkata story and his art of memory and home speak directly to families whose own histories cross Partition and migration.
